questions.request: Hi, I'm doing Paper 2 Topic 10 (authoritarian states) and my case study is Mao's China. In my last practice essay on the Great Leap Forward I basically wrote "millions died because of Mao's bad policies" and got 6/15 - the comment was "no specific evidence, no awareness of debate". Can you explain what actually caused the famine during the Great Leap Forward (1958-62) and how bad it was, but with proper specifics I can use: dates, grain output figures, the actual policies (communes, backyard furnaces, the farming methods etc), named events like the conference where Mao's critic got purged, and the 1962 meeting where someone said it was mostly man-made (who said it?). Most importantly I need the different death toll estimates and WHO gives each one, because I want to write "according to X" instead of just "millions". Also where do historians actually disagree about whose fault it was - Mao personally, the system, local cadres, the weather? Please flag anything that's contested rather than giving me one number as if it's settled. I'm SL so this is for a 15 mark essay.
strong_answer_must: Date the Great Leap Forward precisely: launched 1958 under the Second Five-Year Plan; people's communes generalised after the Beidaihe Politburo resolution of August 1958 (roughly 26,000 communes covering about 99% of rural households by the end of 1958); backyard steel furnaces in autumn 1958 with the steel target doubled to 10.7 million tonnes; retreat and partial decollectivisation 1960-62.

Name the Lushan Conference (July-August 1959) as the event where Defence Minister Peng Dehuai criticised the Leap in a private letter to Mao (14 July 1959), was denounced as leader of an 'anti-Party clique', and was replaced by Lin Biao; explain that the ensuing anti-rightist drive silenced criticism and deepened the famine in 1959-60.

Identify the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference (January-February 1962) and attribute the judgement that the disaster was 'three parts natural calamity, seven parts man-made' to Liu Shaoqi, not Mao; note Mao's limited self-criticism and his withdrawal to the 'second line' while remaining Party Chairman (he had already handed the state chairmanship to Liu in April 1959).

Give grain output figures with a source and flag them as later-revised official statistics: approximately 200 million tonnes in 1958 (against wildly inflated claims of 375 million at the time), falling to about 170 million in 1959 and roughly 143-144 million in 1960, recovering only slowly in 1961 (State Statistical Bureau figures published in the 1980s, used by Western demographers).

Explain the causal mechanism rather than just listing policies: exaggerated reporting ('wind of exaggeration') led to procurement quotas set on fictional harvests, so the state took a rising share of a falling harvest (procurement around a quarter or more of output in 1959) while grain exports continued (several million tonnes in 1959-60); communal mess halls wasted stocks; labour was diverted to steel and irrigation; Lysenko-inspired techniques (close planting, deep ploughing) and the Four Pests campaign reduced yields.

Present the death-toll estimates as a contested range with named authors, not a single number: e.g. Frank Dikötter, Mao's Great Famine (2010), at least 45 million; Yang Jisheng, Tombstone (Chinese 2008, English 2012), about 36 million; Judith Banister (1987) and Basil Ashton et al. (1984) around 30 million; Jasper Becker, Hungry Ghosts (1996), about 30 million; Cao Shuji (2005) around 32.5 million; Peng Xizhe (1987) about 23 million; lower official-leaning Chinese estimates in the mid-teens of millions; and note that some Chinese scholars (e.g. Sun Jingxian) argue for far lower figures and that Cormac O Grada and others have criticised Dikotter's method - the answer must say estimates differ because of baseline mortality assumptions and whether lost births are counted.

Map the historiographical debate on responsibility with attribution: Dikötter (Mao personally, coercion and violence as central); Yang Jisheng (the totalitarian system and cadre terror); the CCP's own 1981 Resolution (leftist errors plus natural disasters, protecting the system); Amartya Sen's argument that famines of this scale do not occur where there is a free press and political opposition (information failure); Thomas Bernstein on excessive procurement; Justin Yifu Lin and Dennis Yang's 'exit rights' argument about communes; the role of provincial leaders such as Wu Zhipu in Henan (Xinyang) and Li Jingquan in Sichuan; and the weather/natural-disaster argument as a minor factor in most Western scholarship.

If it uses the alleged Mao remark from the March 1959 Shanghai meeting about letting 'half the people die', present it as disputed: Dikötter's reading versus critics who argue the remark concerned cutting industrial projects, not people, and that the context is contested.

Model the attribution phrasing the student asked for ('according to Dikötter...', 'Yang Jisheng argues...') and structure the answer as causes, consequences and debate so it can be turned into a 15-mark Paper 2 essay with a clear line of argument.

Explicitly flag which claims are settled (chronology, the Lushan purge, the fall in output) and which are contested (death toll, Mao's knowledge and intent, relative weight of weather), rather than giving one number as if settled.
pitfalls: Giving a single death toll (e.g. '45 million' or '30 million') as established fact without naming who estimates it and why estimates differ.

Misdating Lushan (it was 1959, not 1958 or 1960) or confusing Peng Dehuai with Lin Biao, Liu Shaoqi or Deng Xiaoping; saying Peng was executed (he was purged, later persecuted during the Cultural Revolution and died in 1974).
Attributing 'three parts natural disaster, seven parts man-made' to Mao or Zhou Enlai instead of Liu Shaoqi at the January-February 1962 cadres' conference.
Claiming Mao was removed from power in 1959 or 1962; he gave up the state chairmanship in April 1959 but remained Chairman of the Party.
Conflating the Great Leap Forward with the Hundred Flowers campaign (1956-57), the Anti-Rightist campaign of 1957 or the Cultural Revolution (1966-76).

Fabricating precise grain tonnages, procurement percentages, page numbers or verbatim quotations from historians; inventing historians or books; attributing Tombstone to Dikötter or Mao's Great Famine to Yang.
Quoting the 'half the people die' remark as proof of intent without noting that its interpretation is disputed.
Treating Dikötter's 45 million as the 'accepted' figure, or dismissing lower estimates without explaining the methodological disagreement.
Presenting the weather as the main cause (echoing the 1981 Party line) or ignoring it entirely, rather than weighing it against policy causes with attribution.
Giving a generic moral verdict ('Mao was evil') in place of a causal argument the student can use in a 15-mark essay.

questions.request:
Source A below is a practice source my teacher wrote for Paper 1 (Move to global war - German expansion). She said it is invented but "everything in it is based on something real". I'm HL.

(a) With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a historian studying why Britain and France did not resist the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in March 1936. [4 marks]

(b) Separately, can you fact-check the source for me? Is "nineteen thousand soldiers" right - I've seen 3,000, 22,000 and 30,000 in different places? Did Hitler really say the "tails between our legs" thing, and if so how do we even know - my teacher said some of the quotes in the source are "suspiciously famous" and we should ask where they really come from. Who was the lord with the "back garden" comment? And is it true the French didn't act because of their elections, or is that just the diarist's opinion? I want to know which bits are solid and which bits historians disagree on, so please say where each claim comes from rather than just telling me it's true.

supplied_texts.title: Source A - diary extract (fictional practice source written by the student's teacher)
supplied_texts.text:
Extract from the private diary of Hans-Georg Lindemann, a junior official in the German Foreign Office in Berlin, entry dated Monday 9 March 1936. [Fictional practice source: Lindemann is an invented person and this diary does not exist.]

Two days have passed since our battalions crossed the Rhine bridges at Cologne and Mainz, and still the French have not moved. Neurath told us this morning that Paris will appeal to the League and go to London rather than to the frontier. The Führer, I am told, did not sleep on Saturday night; Blomberg wanted the men back on the east bank the moment a single French division stirred. In the Ministry the joke is that Locarno died in its own bed and nobody sent flowers. The British are the key. Their ambassador said only that the matter must go to the League, and one of their lords is reported to have said that we have merely walked into our own back garden. Nineteen thousand soldiers and some police: that is the whole of our 'invasion', and yet the Paris papers write of a hundred thousand. Let them. The Führer told Neurath that had the French marched we should have had to retreat with our tails between our legs. But they will not march. Their elections come in April, and no Frenchman will die for a treaty his own government has already half abandoned.

strong_answer_must: Treat Source A as what it is - an invented classroom practice source - and say so: it cannot be used as evidence of anything, but it can be analysed as if it were a diary for exam practice, and its claims can be checked against the real record.

For part (a), give a Paper 1 style OPCVL answer that explicitly links value and limitations to origin, purpose and content: value - a contemporary private diary (9 March 1936, two days after the event) by an insider in the German Foreign Office, written for himself rather than for publication, so it is candid about German nervousness (sleepless Hitler, Blomberg wanting to pull back), German troop strength and the German reading of British and French motives; limitations - the author is junior and his information is explicitly second-hand ('I am told', 'reported to have said'), it is a Berlin-centred view that cannot show British or French decision-making from the inside, the tone is boastful and dismissive ('Let them'), and the troop figure and quotations are unverifiable within the source.

Get the core facts right: German troops entered the demilitarised Rhineland on Saturday 7 March 1936, breaching Articles 42-44 of the Treaty of Versailles and the 1925 Locarno Treaty, with the French ratification of the Franco-Soviet pact (Chamber vote 27 February 1936) used as Hitler's pretext; Hitler simultaneously offered a 'peace' package (non-aggression pacts, return to the League).

Answer the troop-number question as a range with attribution and explain why figures differ: only about three battalions (around 3,000 men) advanced deep into the zone (towards Aachen, Trier, Saarbrücken), while roughly 20,000-30,000 soldiers entered the zone in total and about 14,000 Landespolizei were absorbed into the army; French intelligence inflated the figure to well over 200,000 (often cited as 265,000). The answer should name where such figures come from (e.g. Ian Kershaw, Hitler 1889-1936: Hubris; Gerhard Weinberg's work on Hitler's foreign policy; J. T. Emmerson, The Rhineland Crisis 1936) and say the diary's 'nineteen thousand' sits inside the plausible range but is not a verifiable figure.

Trace the 'tails between our legs' quotation to its real provenance: it comes from the post-war memoir of Paul Schmidt, Hitler's interpreter (German edition 1949; English 'Hitler's Interpreter', 1951), who recalled Hitler saying the forty-eight hours after the march were the most nerve-racking of his life and that the Germans would have had to withdraw 'with our tails between our legs' if the French had marched. Point out that it is retrospective hearsay, not a contemporary document, so its appearance in a diary dated 9 March 1936 is the 'suspiciously famous' anachronism the teacher hinted at.

Flag that whether German troops actually had orders to withdraw is itself contested: some historians argue the orders provided for a fighting retreat to defensive positions on the Rhine rather than a full withdrawal, and that Hitler's later claims exaggerated the gamble; Blomberg's nervousness and request to pull back (refused by Hitler) is widely reported but also rests on later testimony.

Identify the 'back garden' remark with Lord Lothian (Philip Kerr), the Liberal peer and former Lloyd George secretary, usually quoted as 'The Germans, after all, are only going into their own back garden', and note that its exact primary provenance is unclear - it circulates mostly through secondary accounts - so the student should cite it cautiously.

Evaluate the elections claim as partly supported but incomplete, with evidence: France had a caretaker government under Albert Sarraut facing general elections on 26 April and 3 May 1936; General Gamelin told ministers that a response required general mobilisation, which the government would not order; French military doctrine was defensive (Maginot Line); Stephen Schuker argued (1986) that the franc and financial crisis constrained France; Britain (Baldwin, Eden) refused to support military action and public opinion favoured negotiation; Foreign Minister Flandin's trip to London (11-12 March) and the League Council meeting in London (14-19 March) produced only a finding that Germany was in breach, with no sanctions; Italy was alienated by Abyssinian sanctions. So 'elections' is one factor among several.

Attribute interpretive claims to historians rather than asserting them: e.g. A. J. P. Taylor (The Origins of the Second World War, 1961) on Hitler as opportunist and the Rhineland as a point at which Hitler could have been stopped cheaply; Churchill's retrospective argument in The Gathering Storm; Kershaw and Weinberg on the gamble and the orders; Schuker on French finances; Emmerson on the crisis diplomacy.

Clearly separate 'solid' claims (date, day of the week, Locarno and Versailles breach, French appeal to the League, French elections in April-May, no military response) from 'contested' ones (troop numbers, withdrawal orders, the provenance and reliability of the famous quotations, the relative weight of elections versus military advice, finance and British attitude).

Say what the student should do in the exam: do not reproduce the famous quotations as established fact; if used, attribute them (e.g. 'according to Schmidt's post-war memoir') and note their limitations.
pitfalls: Treating the fictional diary as a genuine primary source, 'recognising' Lindemann, or inventing biographical details about him.

Asserting a single troop number (e.g. 'exactly 22,000') as fact, or not explaining that different figures count different things (spearhead battalions, total entering the zone, police absorbed, French intelligence estimates).

Attributing the 'tails between our legs' or 'forty-eight hours' remark to Mein Kampf, Hitler's Table Talk, a speech, or a contemporary document, rather than to Paul Schmidt's post-war memoir; or failing to notice the anachronism in a March 1936 diary.
Attributing the 'back garden' remark to Lord Halifax, Neville Chamberlain, Anthony Eden, Stanley Baldwin or Lord Londonderry instead of Lord Lothian, or presenting its provenance as certain.
Saying Léon Blum or the Popular Front was in power in March 1936 (Blum became Prime Minister in June 1936; the Sarraut government was in office during the crisis).

Claiming Britain and France approved the remilitarisation in advance, that the League imposed sanctions, or that France mobilised; confusing Flandin with Laval; placing the League Council meeting in Geneva rather than London, or misdating the crisis to 1935 or 1937.
Stating as proven fact that German commanders had orders to withdraw at the first sign of French resistance, when historians dispute this.
Fabricating page numbers, verbatim quotations or titles for historians; inventing a 'historian' to support a claim.
Answering (a) with a generic 'diaries are biased' template that does not reference the specific origin, purpose and content of Source A, or giving only value or only limitations.
Dismissing the diarist's elections explanation entirely or endorsing it entirely, instead of weighing it against military, financial and British-policy factors with attribution.
